newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Telstra float aimed at small investors.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Telstra float aimed at small investors.

text.p: The Australian government is likely to receive handsome rewards from its plan to target local investors in the upcoming float of the national telephone firm Telstra Corp, analysts said on Monday.
Telstra will be the country's largest privatisation, raising more than A$10 billion (US$7.35 billion) from the sale of one third of the government's stake.
A sharemarket listing is scheduled for November.
The conservative government of Prime Minister John Howard on Sunday launched a campaign to sell at least 65 percent of the shares on offer to the Australian public and institutions.
The government will not sell any more Telstra shares unless it receives a mandate in the next federal election due in 1999.
Analysts said the Australian government's float strategy was similar to that of Britain and Germany.

Last year, the German government sold 23 percent of Deutsche Telekom and in 1984 the British government started its initial sell-down of British Telecommunications Plc. Both floats were led on campaigns aimed at private investors.
"It is a political move. As far as the government is concerned they want every citizen to be a shareholder," said one Sydney-based telecommunications analyst.

"Their goal is to make as many shareholders in Telstra and make them feel good about Telstra. It will provide investors a reasonable return, and the capital gains and the kudos from that will flow on to the government," the analyst said.

The goverment is expected to repeat the success of last year's sale of the final tranche of shares in banking group Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) by using an instalment process, which was hugely popular with Australian investors.
Under this process, investors pay for their shares in two instalments and receive full dividend rights immediately.
Investors who took the CBA instalment approach saw the price of CBA receipts more than double over the past year from the initial payment of A$6.00.

The second CBA instalment payment due in November will coincide with the Telstra float. But analysts said investors will have been saving for both CBA and Telstra investments, helped by strong CBA dividends.
"I would think there are enough mums and dads around to take up this issue. I can't see there being a problem," said the Sydney-based analyst.
The more private investors take of Telstra the more of a squeeze it will be on institutions, analysts said.
"I am sure the mums and dads will love it, I am sure they will buy it and how much is left to the institutions, we have to wait and see," a second Sydney-based analyst said.

Finance Minister John Fahey said on Sunday that at least 65 percent of the shares will be available to Australian public investors and institutions, but did not break down the split, and 3.8 percent would be reserved for Telstra employees.
A television and print advertising campaign to promote the float will begin on August 17. The Telstra prospectus will also be available by phone and through the Internet.
The number of shares which make up subscribers' entitlements will be determined by the overall number of investors who reserve an offer document by September 12, Fahey said.
